statement: Ta'if lies in the hills east of Makkah, home of Thaqif, a fertile town of gardens and vineyards.
notes: Distance given loosely as 'some two days' journey' (about 60 miles).

statement: He went to Ta'if in the tenth year of the mission after Abu Talib's death, with Zayd ibn Harithah, seeking support and protection.
alternatives: Usually dated Shawwal of the tenth year. Some reports say he went alone.

statement: He spoke to three brothers who led Thaqif; they refused and mocked him and did not keep his visit quiet.
notes: Bukhari 3231 confirms the approach to Ibn Abd Yalil and his refusal.

statement: The townspeople were set on him, stoned him until his feet bled; Zayd shielded him and was wounded; they sheltered at an orchard.
The supplication 'O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness' is graded weak.
notes: Editorial statement. Recorded by at-Tabarani; graded da'if by al-Albani (from memory). Reviewer to confirm.

statement: The orchard's owners (Utbah and Shaybah, sons of Rabi'ah) sent their Christian servant Addas of Nineveh with grapes; the exchange about 'In the name of Allah' and Yunus ibn Matta.
notes: From Ibn Ishaq; narrated with 'the report says'. Reviewer to decide whether the quoted words should be kept.

statement: Aishah asked whether any day was harder than Uhud; he described the day of Aqabah, Ibn Abd Yalil's refusal, his grief until Qarn ath-Tha'alib, the cloud and Jibril, the angel of the mountains offering to bring the two mountains upon them, and his reply hoping for descendants who would worship Allah alone.
notes: Direct speech throughout. Machine-checked against Bukhari 3231. The narration does not name Ta'if; the historians identify the occasion.

statement: The jinn listened at Nakhlah during his night prayer on the return from Ta'if.
alternatives: Bukhari 4921 (Ibn Abbas) places the jinn's listening at Nakhlah while he was on the way to the market of Ukaz with Companions; the historians relate an occasion on the return from Ta'if. The two may be separate events.

statement: He sought protection to re-enter Makkah; al-Mut'im ibn Adi, a non-Muslim, armed himself and his sons and announced his protection at the Ka'bah.
After Badr he said that had al-Mut'im ibn Adi been alive and interceded for the captives he would have released them for him.
notes: Machine-checked. That al-Mut'im died before Badr without accepting Islam is from the Seerah.
